    • 8. Properties of the Lebesgue integral

    8. Properties of the Lebesgue integral#

    In the previous note, we constructed the Lebesgue integral for non-negative measurable functions and proved the monotone convergence theorem, which turns pointwise approximation from below into convergence of integrals. In these notes, we first apply monotone convergence to compute the integral of an unbounded function directly, demonstrating that the Lebesgue theory handles singularities without needing a separate framework of improper integrals. We then investigate the structural consequences of having a finite integral. Markov’s inequality provides quantitative control on the measure of superlevel sets, implying in particular that an integrable function is finite almost everywhere. Next, we examine uniform integrability, which shows that a function with finite integral cannot concentrate a positive amount of integral on sets of arbitrarily small measure. Finally, we decompose signed functions into their positive and negative parts to define the Lebesgue integral for general real-valued functions and establish its linearity.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Compute an unbounded Lebesgue integral by superlevel sets and by monotone truncation.

    • Apply Markov’s inequality to estimate the measure of a superlevel set.

    • Explain why every measurable function has integral zero over a null set, even when it takes the value there.

    • Prove that a non-negative function with finite integral has uniformly small integrals over sets of small measure.

    • Define the integral of an integrable signed function and prove its linearity.

    Throughout these notes, denotes a measure space. Unless a signed function is explicitly under discussion, measurable functions take values in .

    Before proving Theorem 8.8, let us describe the strategy of the proof. Uniform integrability is easier to prove for bounded functions, and in particular for simple functions with finite integral, because their values are bounded by a finite maximum . For an arbitrary function with finite integral, we approximate from below by an increasing sequence of non-negative simple functions . By the monotone convergence theorem, the remainder becomes arbitrarily small for large . Because this approximation error is controlled globally on all of , the choice of approximating simple function is not dependent on the set over which we will integrate.
